1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6.name: Old Indian Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6.background: Siegbert Tarrasch introduced it in 1902, but it is more commonly associated with Mikhail Chigorin, who adopted it five years later and pioneered it late in his career. It has never attained the popularity of the King's Indian, though some King's Indian players use it to avoid the Sämisch and Averbakh Variations.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3.strategy: The principal move: it develops a piece towards the centre and prepares e4. White wants a classical pawn centre, and Black has to contest it with pieces and well-timed pawn breaks, since waiting would leave White with much more space.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the kingside knight and covers e5, keeping the choice of set-up open. It claims less space at once than a knight on c3 and leaves Black free to fianchetto the king's bishop or develop it modestly.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.g4.strategy: Offers a pawn with nothing developed to defend it: Black simply takes it with the knight or the bishop. White has loosened the kingside and has little to show for the pawn.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.g4.name: Old Indian Defence: Aged Gibbon Gambit

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 e5.strategy: Occupies the centre with a pawn backed by d6 and challenges White's plan of building a big pawn centre. Black accepts a compact structure with a little less space, but a solid one in which every piece has a clear job.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Bf5.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before it can be shut in, and stops White's space grab: 4.e4 would simply lose a pawn to ...Nxe4. The price is that the bishop on f5 needs care later, and Black still has to settle the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nbd7.strategy: Develops the knight to support ...e5 and keeps the c-pawn free. It is a flexible, solid choice, but White can take the full centre at once, so Black accepts being a little cramped.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 c6.strategy: A solid, flexible move: the c6 pawn takes d5 and b5 from White's pieces and keeps ...e5 in reserve. It takes the natural square c6 from the queen's knight and leaves White the first say in the centre.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 c6.name: Old Indian Defence: Czech Variation, with Nc3

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nf3 Bg4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and attacks the knight on f3, which guards d4 and e5. Black can trade it off, and a pawn recapture would double White's pawns, so Black develops with a small threat and keeps the centre contested.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nf3 Bg4.name: Old Indian Defence: Tartakower-Indian

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nf3 c6.strategy: Prepares a solid centre with a pawn on c6 that takes d5 and b5 from White's pieces. It takes the natural square from the queen's knight and does not challenge White's centre, so Black waits to see what White does.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6 3.Nf3 c6.name: Old Indian Defence: Czech Variation, with Nf3
